section.title: To Live Is Christ
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns from prayer to his own imprisonment and shows how God has used even chains to advance the gospel. Whether preachers act from goodwill or rivalry, Christ is proclaimed and Paul rejoices. The section climbs to the letter's most famous confession, to live is Christ and to die is gain, where Paul weighs death against continued service and chooses whatever most magnifies Christ and helps the church.
section.thesis: Paul's imprisonment has served to advance the gospel and embolden others to preach, so that whether by false motive or true Christ is proclaimed and Paul rejoices; and because for him to live is Christ and to die is gain, he faces death without fear, longing to be with Christ yet content to remain for the sake of the Philippians' progress and joy in the faith.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the gospel advancing through Paul's chains; his joy that Christ is preached whatever the motive; and the confession that to live is Christ and to die is gain, resolved in staying for the church's sake.

verses.text: Now I want you to know, brothers, that my circumstances have actually served to {{prokope|advance}} the gospel.
As a result, it has become clear throughout the whole {{praitorion|palace guard}} and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ.
And most of the brothers, confident in the Lord by my chains, now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear.

units.label: Christ preached, and Paul rejoices
units.note: whether by false motive or true

verses.text: It is true that some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.
The latter do so in love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel.
The former, however, preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains.
What then is the issue? Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will continue to rejoice,
because I know that through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, my distress will turn out for my deliverance.
I eagerly expect and hope that I will in no way be ashamed, but will have complete boldness so that now as always Christ will be {{megalyno|exalted}} in my body, whether by life or by death.

units.label: To live is Christ, to die is gain
units.note: torn between two, staying for their sake

verses.text: For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is {{kerdos|gain}}.
But if I go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labor for me. So what shall I choose? I do not know.
I am torn between the two. I desire to {{analyo|depart}} and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.
But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.
Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith,
so that through my coming to you again your exultation in Christ Jesus will resound on account of me.

prokope.gloss: Advance, progress, a going forward, a word used of an army cutting a path ahead. Paul says his imprisonment has not hindered but advanced the gospel; what looked like a setback became a road for the good news to press forward into the palace guard and beyond.

praitorion.gloss: The Praetorium, the imperial guard or governor's headquarters. Paul's chains put him in daily contact with elite Roman soldiers, and through them the reason for his imprisonment, Christ, became known throughout the guard. The gospel reached the very heart of Roman power through a prisoner.

megalyno.gloss: To magnify, to make great, to exalt. Paul's single ambition is that Christ be magnified in his body, whether he lives or dies. His life is not about his own vindication but about displaying the greatness of Christ, in freedom or in death, with complete boldness.

kerdos.gloss: Gain, profit, advantage. To die is gain because death ushers the believer into the immediate presence of Christ, which Paul calls far better. Death is not loss for the Christian but the doorway to the greatest possible profit, being with the Lord he loves.

analyo.gloss: To depart, to loosen, as of a ship casting off its moorings or a soldier striking camp. Paul pictures death not as extinction but as departure, a setting sail to be with Christ. The word gives death the character of a journey home rather than an end.

basic.context: Paul writes from prison, and the Philippians are worried for him. He reassures them: far from silencing him, his chains have pushed the gospel forward. The palace guard now knows why he is imprisoned, and other believers are speaking more boldly. Some preach from bad motives, some from good, but Christ is preached, and that is enough to make Paul rejoice. Then he opens his heart: living means Christ, dying means gain, and he will gladly stay to help this church grow.
basic.hermeneutics: This is autobiography with a purpose. Paul turns his own hard circumstances into an example, teaching the Philippians how to face suffering, rivalry, and even death with joy centered on Christ. The famous line of verse 21 is not a slogan but the settled conviction of a man in chains.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul's chains led to the prokope, the advance, of the gospel, even into the praitorion, the palace guard. His one aim is that Christ be megalyno, magnified, in his body by life or death. To die is kerdos, gain, and he longs to analyo, to depart, like a ship casting off, and be with Christ.
basic.typology: Paul's willingness to be poured out for the gospel and to count death as gain follows the pattern of Christ Himself, who through death won life for many. The suffering servant who does not shrink from shame but trusts God to vindicate him is echoed in Paul's confident hope that he will not be put to shame.
basic.christ: Christ is everything here: the content of all true preaching, the one to be magnified in Paul's body, the whole meaning of Paul's living, and the joy that makes his dying gain. To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better than anything this life offers. Christ is both the reason to live and the reward of death.
basic.god: God is at work behind the scenes, turning imprisonment into gospel advance and even mixed motives into the spread of Christ's name. The Spirit of Jesus Christ supplies Paul in his distress. God is sovereign over Paul's chains and over his life and death, and works all of it for His glory and the church's good.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8:28 says God works all things for good. 2 Corinthians 5:8 speaks of being away from the body and at home with the Lord. Acts 16 tells of the founding of the Philippian church in the shadow of a prison.
basic.oneStory: God has always advanced His purposes through the suffering of His servants, and supremely through the death of His Son. Here Paul joins that story: his chains carry the gospel forward, and his readiness to die for Christ points to the hope of resurrection life secured by Christ's own death and rising.

context.literary:
Philippians 1:12 to 26 is the first body paragraph of the letter, and it is largely autobiography with a lesson folded inside. It opens with a disclosure formula, 'Now I want you to know,' that ancient letters used to introduce news, and the news is the opposite of what the Philippians fear: Paul's circumstances have served the gospel. The passage then moves in three waves. Verses 12 to 18a report on the effect of his chains, first on the guard and the city, then on the other believers, then on rival preachers. Verses 18b to 26 turn to the future, first his hope of deliverance and boldness, then the choice between living and dying, and last the conviction that he will remain for their joy.

The passage is held together by repetition. 'Christ' appears in almost every verse, and the climactic confession of verse 21 is a sentence with no verbs: to me the living Christ, and the dying gain. 'Rejoice' sounds twice in verse 18, the second time looking forward. A set of word pairs structures the argument: life and death, body and absence from it, Paul's good and the Philippians' good, 'to stay' and 'to depart.' The paragraph resolves not with a decision but with a conviction, which is typical of Paul's way of reasoning here: he does not know what he would choose, and he sets personal preference below the church's need.

In the letter's wider structure, this section does two jobs. It reassures the Philippians that they need not be anxious about their apostle, and it displays an attitude toward suffering and rivalry that Paul will ask them to share. The self-forgetfulness shown in verses 15 to 18 will be commanded in 2:3 and 4 and embodied in Christ in 2:6 to 8.
context.historical:
Paul writes from custody, probably in Rome in the early 60s, where Acts 28:30 and 31 says he stayed two years in a rented house, welcoming visitors and proclaiming the kingdom boldly. Acts 28:16 says a soldier guarded him, and that is the likely background to the remark in verse 13 that it has become clear throughout the whole praetorian guard that he is in chains for Christ. Soldiers who rotated through his guard duty would have heard his story and his message at close quarters.

The praitorion in verse 13 can mean the elite guard attached to the emperor or the headquarters where it was housed. In either case the gospel is reaching the heart of the imperial system, and by 4:22 the greeting will mention believers 'from the household of Caesar.' This is how a movement spread in Paul's world: through networks of soldiers, slaves, officials and merchants who knew each other and moved around the empire.

The rivalry in verses 15 to 17 is a window into the Roman church. Paul does not say who the rivals were, and nothing in the text suggests they preached a false gospel. Their sin was in the heart. It is quite possible they were Christians who envied Paul's reputation or resented his prominence and who thought they could use his imprisonment to raise their own standing. Paul's death, in verse 20 and following, was a real possibility. A Roman trial of this sort could end in release or execution, and the emperor's court was unpredictable. Verse 19's 'distress will turn out for my deliverance' is a hope, not a prediction, and verses 20 to 26 hold both outcomes open.
context.canonical:
Several Old Testament texts stand behind this passage. Verse 19 closely echoes the Greek of Job 13:16, where Job, in great distress and defending himself before God, says that this will be his salvation. Job's confidence that God will vindicate him in the end, even if God slays him, Job 13:15 and 19:25 to 27, becomes Paul's confidence. The verb of being ashamed in verse 20 recalls the psalmist's repeated prayer not to be put to shame, as in Psalm 25:2 and 3, and Isaiah 50:7, where the Servant says he knows he will not be ashamed.

The theme of God turning evil to good runs from Genesis 50:20, where Joseph tells his brothers that what they intended for evil God intended for good, through Romans 8:28. Paul's chains function in this way. They are a Joseph-like reversal in which his imprisonment advances the very cause the authorities meant to stop. The way Paul rejoices that Christ is preached even by rivals also recalls Moses' reaction to Eldad and Medad, Numbers 11:26 to 29, and Jesus' answer to John in Mark 9:38 to 40, 'whoever is not against us is for us.'

Verses 21 to 23 are among the Bible's clearest statements about the believer's state at death. Jesus tells the thief, 'today you will be with Me in Paradise,' Luke 23:43. Paul says elsewhere that to be 'away from the body' is to be 'at home with the Lord,' 2 Corinthians 5:6 to 8, and that those who sleep in death will be brought with Jesus, 1 Thessalonians 4:13 and 14. 2 Timothy 4:6 to 8 is the same man looking again at the same departure, near the end of his life, and finding it a crown.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wrote to answer a real fear. The Philippians had heard that he was in prison, and they had sent money and a messenger, Epaphroditus. News of Paul's condition would reach them in a letter, and he decided to use it to change how they think about suffering. He gave a firsthand report that the gospel had advanced because of his chains, and that the brothers and sisters in the city had become bolder. Paul wanted the church to learn that the cause of Christ does not rise and fall with the safety of its leaders.

He also wanted to model a joy that does not depend on being treated fairly. Verse 18 is not an indifference to truth; it is a settled refusal to let envy and ambition, his own or others', become the centre. He then put his own life on the table: if he lives, it is for Christ and for them, and if he dies, it is gain. The point is that a person for whom Christ is everything has nothing to fear from either result. That is an unspoken invitation to the Philippians, who face their own pressures from outside the church and from within, 1:28 to 30, to find in Christ the same security.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is descriptive, a report on Paul's circumstances, motives and hopes. Verse 21 is a personal confession, not a command, and the passage never says 'you must regard death as gain.' It becomes prescriptive by example, as Paul invites the church to follow his pattern, 3:17, and to share his disposition, 2:5.

Two cautions apply. First, Paul's longing to depart is not an endorsement of a morbid wish to die. He weighs the choice and sets it aside for the church's good, and Scripture elsewhere honours life as a gift and forbids taking it into one's own hands. The statement is about where the believer's security lies, not about hastening death. Second, verse 19 is a hope formed in prayer, not a guarantee of release. Paul does not say how the trial would end, so the passage cannot be used to promise believers that suffering will end in rescue on earth. What is promised is that Christ will be honoured, and that either outcome is good.

debates.question: Should Paul rejoice that rivals preach Christ from bad motives?

views.label: He rejoices that Christ is preached, not in their sin
views.case: Paul distinguishes the message from the motive; the true gospel is going out, and he rejoices in that, while still naming the envy and selfish ambition as wrong.

views.label: He commends their motives
views.case: This misreads the text; Paul plainly calls their motive envy, rivalry, and selfish ambition, and rejoices only that Christ is nonetheless proclaimed.

debates.bearing: Paul's joy is anchored in the spread of Christ's name, not in approving of impure motives; the gospel is bigger than its flawed messengers.

debates.question: What does Paul expect at death, and what is the state of believers who die?

views.label: Immediate presence with Christ
views.case: To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better; Paul expects conscious fellowship with the Lord at death, awaiting the resurrection of the body.

views.label: Only a future resurrection with no interim
views.case: Some stress the resurrection so strongly they downplay the interim; yet Paul's far better presses for a real gain at death itself, being with Christ.

debates.bearing: The verse gives comfort that death brings the believer into Christ's presence, the intermediate joy that precedes the resurrection of the body.

debates.question: Is Paul describing a conscious state with Christ immediately at death?

views.label: Yes: the intermediate state is conscious fellowship
views.case: The verb 'depart' and the phrase 'with Christ' are joined to 'far better,' which only makes sense if the departed are with Him. Luke 23:43, 2 Corinthians 5:8 and Revelation 6:9 to 11 are read the same way. Most of the church's tradition holds this.

views.label: Death as sleep until the resurrection, with no experienced interval
views.case: Some argue that for the dead there is no passing of time, so that departure and being with Christ are, from the believer's side, the next moment after death, with the resurrection following immediately in experience. They appeal to Paul's frequent use of 'sleep' for the dead, 1 Thessalonians 4:13, and to the weight of 1 Corinthians 15.

debates.bearing: Both views take Paul at his word that the believer's death is gain and is a going to Christ. They differ about how to describe the interval, and the text does not settle that. What it settles is that nothing in death separates the believer from the Lord.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul begins by calling the Philippians adelphoi, brothers, a word that in his letters includes the whole family of the church, sisters as well, and the opening in verse 12 is a formula for introducing news. The word for his chains, desmoi in verse 13, 14 and 17, is the plural of bonds, and Paul uses it as a badge: they are 'chains in Christ,' en Christo, meaning his imprisonment is part of belonging to Christ and is known as such.

In verses 15 to 18 the verb for preaching is kataggello, to announce publicly, used of both rivals and friends. It is the same verb in both cases, and Paul keeps the content, Christ, steady while the motives change. The noun for the rivals' ambition is eritheia, a word that means selfish rivalry or party spirit; the same word returns at 2:3 where Paul commands the church to do nothing out of it. The word has a political ring, as of someone working for their own faction, and Paul uses it to expose the way a gospel messenger can serve himself. The noun 'goodwill,' eudokia, is the opposite, a gladness in God's purposes. In verse 18 the question 'what then?' (ti gar) invites a conclusion, and Paul gives it.

Verse 19 is one of the closest echoes of the Greek Old Testament in the letter. 'Will turn out for my deliverance' is touto moi apobesetai eis soterian, nearly the same words as Job 13:16 in the Septuagint. The word soteria, usually 'salvation,' means here the final vindication, as in Job's case, and not an acquittal in court. 'The provision of the Spirit' is epichoregia, a supply or support, the noun that comes from the verb for supplying a chorus at one's own cost, and Ephesians 4:16 uses it for the supporting ligaments of the body. The Spirit is the support Paul draws on.

Verse 20 piles up expectation. 'Eager expectation' is apokaradokia, a compound that suggests craning the neck to see what is coming, found also at Romans 8:19. 'Boldness' is parresia, free speech, and 'exalted' translates a verb at the heart of the paragraph, megalyno, so the boldness is for the sake of making Christ great. Verse 21 sets 'to live' as a present continuous action beside 'to die' in a single decisive aorist, as if to say that living is an ongoing daily thing and dying a single event that can only be gain.

In verse 23 'torn' is synechomai, to be held or pressed from two sides, the verb Jesus uses of His own distress at Luke 12:50 and Paul uses of Christ's love at 2 Corinthians 5:14. The pressure comes from two desires, one to depart and one to stay. In verse 26, 'exultation' is kauchema, a ground for boasting, and the boast is in Christ Jesus, not in Paul.

typology.type: Job's vindication, Job 13:15 to 16 and 19:25 to 27
typology.fulfillment: Job, sitting in suffering and defending his integrity, declares that this will be his salvation and that his Redeemer lives. Paul in chains borrows his words in verse 19 and relies on the same hope. The correspondence is of the suffering believer who trusts God to vindicate him. The escalation is in Christ, who is the righteous sufferer vindicated by resurrection, Romans 1:4 and 1 Timothy 3:16, so that the believer's vindication is a share in His. The type falls short because Job's vindication was in this life and Paul's may be through death.

typology.type: Joseph's imprisonment turned to good, Genesis 50:20
typology.fulfillment: Joseph was sold and jailed by those who meant harm, yet God used his chains to preserve many lives. Philippians 1:12 to 14 shows the same pattern at work in Paul, where bonds that were meant to silence the gospel carried it into the imperial guard. The fulfilment in Christ is that the greatest wrong, the cross, became the greatest good, Acts 2:23 and 24. The type is imperfect because Joseph's rescue came in time, but Christ's came by resurrection, and Paul's by a hope still to be seen.

typology.type: Moses and the unjealous leader, Numbers 11:26 to 29
typology.fulfillment: When Eldad and Medad prophesied outside the tent, Joshua asked Moses to stop them, and Moses answered with a wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. Paul's joy that Christ is preached by rivals is the same unjealous spirit. The correspondence is of a leader whose joy is in God's work rather than in his own place. The escalation is that Christ Himself told His disciples not to stop one who was acting in His name, Mark 9:38 to 40, and in Pentecost the Spirit is placed on all God's people, Acts 2:17 and 18. The type falls short in that Moses' wish was a hope, but the Spirit is now given.

study.christ:
The passage speaks of Christ more than of anything else, and it does so in a pattern that deepens as it moves. In verses 12 to 18 Christ is the content of the message: whatever the messengers' motives, 'Christ is preached.' Paul's joy is not in his own reputation or in the purity of the preachers. It is in the fact that a person is being announced to the world, and that person is bigger than the messengers.

In verses 19 and 20 Christ is the one who is to be honoured in Paul's body. 'The Spirit of Jesus Christ' supplies him, a striking name for the Spirit that links the Spirit's work with the Lord's own life, as in Acts 16:7 and Romans 8:9. Paul's body, chained and perhaps soon beheaded, is the stage on which Christ will be made great. 2 Corinthians 4:10 and 11 says the same: the life of Jesus is made visible in a mortal body that always carries the death of Jesus.

In verse 21 Christ is the meaning of life. 'To live is Christ' is a claim that every part of Paul's life has Christ as its content, aim and sustenance, as Galatians 2:20 says, 'Christ lives in me.' It is the reason death is gain and not loss: when a person's life consists in Christ, death takes nothing that matters and brings the person into His presence. Verse 23 supplies the destination. To 'be with Christ' is the fulfilment of Jesus' own promise in John 14:3, that He will take His people to be where He is, and in John 17:24, where He prays that those given to Him may be with Him to see His glory.

There is also a pattern Christ sets. Paul chooses staying for the sake of others, in verse 24, 'it is more necessary for you,' and that choice previews the mind of Christ in 2:5 to 8, who put others' needs ahead of His own comfort. The apostle's weighing of his options is a small copy of the Lord's greater self-giving, Mark 10:45.

Finally the passage offers a resource for the church's grief. Christ has gone through death and out the other side, and so Paul can speak of it as a departure and not an ending. Hebrews 2:14 and 15 says that by His death He freed those who were held in slavery by the fear of death, and Paul's calm in verses 21 to 23 is evidence of it.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who is sovereign over circumstances that look like defeat. Paul does not say that his imprisonment is good in itself. He says that it has 'served to advance the gospel,' and he attributes that outcome, without argument, to a purpose larger than the Roman authorities. This is the same God who turned Joseph's slavery into the preservation of many lives, Genesis 50:20, and who works 'all things' together for good for those who love Him, Romans 8:28. The Philippians are meant to see a God whose hand is on the jailer's keys.

He is also a God who works through flawed instruments. Paul reports that some preach out of envy and yet Christ is preached. God's purposes do not depend on the purity of the preachers, and neither does His gospel's power, for it is the message and not the messenger that saves. This is a mercy, because every church is led by people with mixed motives. It is also a warning, since Paul does not therefore excuse envy. God can use a bad motive without approving it.

The Spirit is presented as a real source of help. 'The provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ' is supplied to Paul in his distress, which means the Spirit is not an abstract power but a personal helper who is connected to Christ. The Philippians' prayers and the Spirit's provision work together, and God ordinarily gives help through both. God is therefore a God who hears the prayers of ordinary church members for a prisoner they have never seen in chains.

God's glory is the goal. Paul's greatest hope is that Christ will be exalted, and that is a way of saying that God is to be honoured. The passage exposes a God who is at once sovereign and personal, who rules prisons and pays attention to the details of a church's anxiety. It also shows what the proper response is: not controlling the outcome but receiving whichever result God gives, 'by life or by death,' with confidence that God's own name is safe. For worship, the passage invites believers to pray for those in custody, to honour God in the face of both the good and the bad and to trust Him with life and death.

crossReferences.note: Job says that even if God slays him he will hope in Him, and that this will be his salvation. Philippians 1:19 echoes the Greek of verse 16 almost word for word, which shows Paul reading his own trial as a Job-like case in which God will vindicate the righteous sufferer.

Joseph tells his brothers that what they intended for evil God intended for good, to preserve many lives. It supplies the pattern for Philippians 1:12 to 14, where Paul's chains advance the gospel, and shows that God's hidden purpose is often in plain view only afterwards.
A promise with no exceptions for the people who love God. The report that the guard heard and the believers grew bolder is a worked example, and it accounts for Paul's calm while chained.

Luke records that Paul stayed two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came and proclaiming the kingdom of God 'boldly and freely.' It confirms what Philippians says about his imprisonment, that the gospel was not bound, and it supplies the historical setting of the letter.

Paul is confident and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord. Philippians 1:23 states the same preference, so the two passages together show that Paul's view of death was consistent: while at home in the body, away from the Lord, but death brings the believer into His presence.

Paul says he is already being poured out like a drink offering and the time of his departure is at hand, then looks to the crown of righteousness. It reads like the other end of Philippians 1:21 to 24, the same man facing the same departure after years, and it shows that the choice he weighed was answered.

Jesus promises the dying thief that today he will be with Him in Paradise. The words give the Lord's own warrant for Paul's confidence that death brings immediate presence with Christ, and they come from a man who, like Paul, had nothing left but the Saviour.

'Christ lives in me' is Paul's other way of saying 'to live is Christ.' Together they show that the apostle's life had Christ as its power and purpose, so that giving up that life for Christ's sake was no loss.

Moses answers Joshua's complaint about Eldad and Medad with the wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. It is the nearest Old Testament parallel to Paul's rejoicing at the preaching of rivals, as it shows the same unjealous joy in God's work spreading outside one's own circle.

John wants to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus' name because he does not follow with them, and Jesus says not to stop him, for whoever is not against us is for us. It gives the Lord's own teaching behind Paul's attitude toward rivals in Philippians 1:18.

study.oneStory:
The question this passage answers is one that every part of Scripture meets sooner or later: what happens to the work of God when His servants suffer? The story begins with a world made good and a human race that chose to live without God, and the consequence was suffering and death, Genesis 3:16 to 19. From that point forward God's purposes move through weakness: Abraham's childlessness, Joseph's prison, Israel's slavery, David's flight, the prophets' rejection and the exile. In each case the plan went forward through the suffering, not despite it.

Philippians 1 stands in the line that leads to the cross. The Servant of Isaiah 53 'poured out His life unto death,' Isaiah 53:12, and the gospel that Paul preaches is the report of that death and its triumph. If the Lord Himself brought life through death, His servants should not be surprised to find that their chains and wounds advance His cause. Paul's own pattern, 'to live is Christ and to die is gain,' is a miniature of what the gospel promises all believers, that their deaths will be a coming into the presence of the one they love.

The passage also touches the church's mission. In the book of Acts the gospel moves from Jerusalem to Rome, and it does so through arrests, trials and shipwrecks. Acts ends with Paul in Rome, 'boldly and freely' proclaiming the kingdom, Acts 28:31, which is the same scene from the other side. Philippians shows what that proclamation looked like to the people involved: believers were growing bolder and soldiers were hearing.

It looks ahead to the new creation too. The 'far better' of verse 23 is a foretaste, as Paul says elsewhere, of what comes when 'the dead in Christ will rise first,' 1 Thessalonians 4:16, and the body is made like His glorious body, Philippians 3:21. In Revelation 21:4 death will be no more. Paul's view is the Christian's anticipation of that day: gain at death, glory at the resurrection, and in the meantime, life as a gift to be spent for others.

quiz.q: What effect did Paul's imprisonment actually have on the gospel?

options.text: It advanced the gospel, making Christ known even in the palace guard.
options.note: Verses 12 to 13 say his chains served to advance the gospel.

options.text: It brought the gospel to a standstill.
options.note: The opposite: Paul says his circumstances advanced the gospel.

options.text: It made the other believers too afraid to speak.
options.note: Verse 14 says most brothers grew bolder, not more afraid.

options.text: It caused Paul to abandon his faith.
options.note: Paul's faith and joy only deepened in prison.

quiz.q: Why can Paul rejoice even when some preach Christ from bad motives?

options.text: Because Christ is still being proclaimed, whatever the motive.
options.note: Verse 18: whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached, and Paul rejoices.

options.text: Because he thinks their envy is admirable.
options.note: He rejoices that Christ is preached, not in their envy or ambition.

options.text: Because their preaching does not really matter.
options.note: It matters greatly; that is why the spread of Christ brings him joy.

options.text: Because he enjoys competition for its own sake.
options.note: His joy is in Christ being preached, not in rivalry.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by to live is Christ and to die is gain?

options.text: Living means serving and knowing Christ, and dying means being with Him, which is better still.
options.note: Verses 21 to 23 hold living for Christ and dying to be with Him together as gain.

options.text: That life is meaningless and only death matters.
options.note: Paul values remaining for fruitful labor; life for Christ is deeply meaningful.

options.text: That Christians should seek death quickly.
options.note: Paul chooses to remain for the church's sake; he does not seek to hasten death.

options.text: That death is simply the end of everything.
options.note: Death is gain because it means being with Christ, not extinction.

quiz.q: Why does Paul expect to remain rather than depart?

options.text: Because it is more necessary for the Philippians' progress and joy in the faith.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25 have Paul stay for the church's good.

options.text: Because he is afraid to die.
options.note: He is not afraid; he even prefers to depart and be with Christ.

options.text: Because he doubts there is life after death.
options.note: He is sure death means being with Christ, far better.

options.text: Because he wants to avoid all suffering.
options.note: He stays to serve, not to escape hardship.

quiz.q: What is Paul's single ambition in life and death?

options.text: That Christ would be magnified in his body, whether by life or death.
options.note: Verse 20 states his aim, that Christ be exalted in him either way.

options.text: That he would be released and honored.
options.note: His concern is Christ's honor, not his own release or reputation.

options.text: That his rivals would be silenced.
options.note: He rejoices that Christ is preached even by rivals.

options.text: That he would be remembered as a great man.
options.note: He wants Christ, not himself, to be magnified.

questions: Paul saw his imprisonment as a way the gospel could advance. Where might God be using a hard circumstance in your life to move the gospel forward?
Paul rejoiced that Christ was preached even by rivals. What would it take for you to care more about Christ being known than about who gets the credit?
For Paul, to live is Christ. If you finished that sentence honestly, to live is what, what would you say, and what would you want to change?
Paul faced death as gain because it meant being with Christ. How does that hope change the way you think about your own death?
Paul chose to stay for the good of others rather than his own comfort. Whose progress and joy in the faith is God calling you to serve?

translationNotes.note: Palace guard renders praitorion; a footnote in the BSB notes the alternative all the Praetorium, the imperial guard or governor's headquarters.
Deliverance translates soteria, which can mean rescue or salvation; Paul echoes Job 13:16 and may intend both his vindication and his final salvation.
Depart renders analyo, to loose or cast off, the image of a ship leaving harbor or a tent being struck, picturing death as departure to be with Christ.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Philippians 1:12-26 this session.
